analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a warrant before tracking someone's phone location and bars companies from sharing it.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by a Republican with Democratic support, never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for the rest of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a crime for anyone to secretly intercept or share another person's phone or GPS location data, with up to five years in prison. It would have required police and intelligence agencies to get a judge's warrant before obtaining someone's location records, allowed warrantless tracking only in emergencies like a kidnapping, and let people sue for damages when their location was illegally tracked. It also would have barred illegally obtained location data from being used as evidence.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who carries a cell phone or GPS device. The bill would have required a warrant before the government could obtain a person's location information, restricted phone and tech companies from deliberately divulging a customer's location, and given individuals the right to sue violators for actual damages plus the violator's profits, or statutory damages of at least $10,000, along with attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who carries a cell phone

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to intentionally intercept, disclose, or use another person's geolocation information obtained in violation of the act [S2][S3].

Requires a search warrant under the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure before a government entity can acquire or compel disclosure of geolocation information, with a narrow emergency exception requiring a court application within 48 hours [S2][S3].

Prohibits providers of electronic communication, remote computing, or geolocation services from intentionally divulging a customer's location information, with exceptions for consent, emergencies, and legal process [S3].

Lets any person whose location information was illegally intercepted or disclosed sue for the greater of actual damages plus the violator's profits, or at least $10,000 in statutory damages, plus attorney's fees, and triggers administrative discipline for willful violations by federal officers [S3].
Bars illegally acquired geolocation information, and evidence derived from it, from being used in any federal, state, or local proceeding [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wireless carriers, tech companies, and any business providing mapping, GPS, or communication services would face criminal liability and lawsuits if they share customers' location data without consent or legal process. Law enforcement agencies would have to obtain warrants for location tracking instead of using subpoenas or informal requests, adding time and judicial review to investigations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Phone carriers, tech firms, police agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves large carve-outs: foreign intelligence surveillance under FISA, information captured in the normal course of a provider's business, consent, public data, and emergencies are all exempt, so much government surveillance could continue [S2][S3].

Civil liability includes statutory damages of the greater of $100 per day or $10,000, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, which could expose service providers to costly litigation over routine data-handling disputes [S3].

Because warrantless location tracking would be barred except in emergencies, investigators lose a faster route to location records, though the emergency exception covers imminent danger of death or serious injury [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are broad and apply to nearly everyone, while the costs fall mainly on companies whose location-data practices the bill would restrict and on investigators who would need warrants. The main design weakness is that the FISA and business exceptions still allow substantial warrantless tracking, so the bill would not have closed the gap as fully as its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees the day it was introduced, sent to a Judiciary crime subcommittee a month later, and never brought up for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jason Chaffetz introduced the bill on January 22, 2015, joined by Representatives Peter Welch and John Conyers [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence [S1][S5].
Four members cosponsored the bill: three Democrats and one Republican [S4].

On February 19, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; no further action appears in the record, and the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phone and internet companies kept the ability to collect and share customers' location data without federal criminal liability, and law enforcement and intelligence agencies continued to obtain location records without a warrant requirement. No one else gained from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a Republican with two original Democratic co-leads, and its four cosponsors split 3-1 between Democrats and Republicans; no vote was ever taken, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Wireless carriers and geolocation service providers
industries.note: The bill would have made it a crime, with up to five years in prison, for these companies to intentionally divulge a customer's location information outside narrow exceptions. That restricted a practice through which customer location data moves to other parties without a warrant or the customer's knowledge.

industries.industry: Tech and remote computing companies handling location data
industries.note: Providers of remote computing and electronic communication services would have faced the same prohibition on divulging location data and exposure to civil damages of at least $10,000 per violation. Their interest in monetizing location data ran against the privacy interest of the people being located.

The bill would have required a warrant for law enforcement to acquire location records, slowing some investigations, but preserved emergency exceptions and the full FISA foreign-intelligence framework. Ordinary people would have gained a warrant requirement while agencies kept substantial surveillance authority.
